secondaryKeywords: how to evaluate an seo quote
h1: How to compare three SEO proposals that look nothing alike
metaTitle: How to Compare SEO Proposals That Look Different
metaDescription: How to compare SEO proposals: turn vague deliverables into hours, put every quote on one sheet, score eight weighted criteria, spot the disqualifier.
answer: Convert every proposal into hours before you compare anything. Phrases like "unlimited keywords" and "20 backlinks a month" aren't units — turn them into working hours, divide by the fee to get a blended rate, then score all three against eight weighted criteria. Any proposal with no baseline is disqualified.
takeaways: Nobody quotes in the same units, so the first job is arithmetic, not judgement. **Hours per rupee** is the only common denominator.
"Unlimited keywords" is worth zero points. Keyword tracking is free; the work isn't.
Thirty backlinks a month at ₹25,000 is arithmetically impossible with earned links. Something else is being sold to you.
One omission disqualifies a proposal regardless of price: **no baseline number, frozen before work starts**.

sections.h2: Three quotes, three sets of units
body: You asked three agencies for a proposal. One came back with a keyword count. One came back with a deliverables list. One came back with a team structure and a number of hours. The fees are ₹25,000, ₹95,000 and ₹75,000, and there is no honest way to say which is cheapest, because they aren't quoting the same thing.
The examples below are composites — the three shapes we see most often in the Indian market, not real quotes from real agencies. Use them as a template for your own three.

The method has three steps: convert deliverables to hours, normalise all three onto one sheet, then score. It takes about ninety minutes and it's the highest-return ninety minutes in the whole buying process. Do it before the follow-up calls, not after — once you've met the people, you'll be scoring how much you liked them, and likeability is uncorrelated with whether your organic leads move.
bullets: **Proposal A — ₹25,000/mo.** Unlimited keywords, 30 backlinks a month, 8 blogs, monthly technical audit, dedicated account manager.
**Proposal B — ₹95,000/mo.** Four long-form articles, technical SEO retained, links via "digital PR", quarterly strategy review, 12-month term.

**Proposal C — ₹75,000/mo.** 45–60 hours itemised by discipline, three named people, sample of the last 20 links placed, month-to-month after the first quarter, one measured number written into the contract.

sections.h2: Step one: turn every phrase into hours
body: Proposals are written in marketing units. Delivery happens in hours. These are reasonable conversions for competent work in India — argue with the numbers, but make the agency argue with them too.

callout.title: Do the backlink arithmetic in front of them
callout.body: Thirty earned links a month is 90–240 hours of outreach. At ₹25,000, that values a working hour at roughly ₹100–₹280. Nobody in India delivers senior outreach at that rate. The links are bought — [which Google counts as link spam](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies) — directory-grade, or they aren't coming. Ask for the last twenty URLs they placed and check them yourself.

sections.h2: Step two: put all three on one sheet
body: Now every proposal is expressed the same way. This is usually the moment the cheap one stops looking cheap and the expensive one stops looking expensive.

Build it as a spreadsheet with the quotes as columns and these seven rows. It takes twenty minutes and it does something no amount of reading can: it forces each agency's claims into a form where they can contradict each other. Proposal A's blended rate is the giveaway — nobody in India staffs senior outreach at ₹180 an hour, so either the deliverables mean something other than what they say, or somebody didn't do the arithmetic before sending the document.

sections.h2: The eight criteria, and what each weight is doing
body: Weights matter more than scores. Most buyers weight price at 40% and measurement at nothing, which is exactly backwards — price is the one variable you can renegotiate later, and measurement is the one you can't retrofit. Score each criterion 1 to 5, multiply by the weight, add it up.

body: Run the composites through it and the ranking inverts against price in one case and confirms it in another.

**Proposal A** scores in the low twenties out of 100. Not because ₹25,000 is too little money — a small local site can genuinely be served at that number — but because every line is unfalsifiable. Unlimited keywords, unnamed writers, unsourced links, no baseline. There is nothing in the document you could later prove they didn't do.

**Proposal B** lands somewhere in the high fifties. The rate is real, the work is probably real, and the people might be excellent. It loses on two things: no baseline, so nobody can say at month nine whether it worked, and a 12-month lock-in that removes your only real remedy. Fixable — ask them to add a measured number and cut the term to six months. If they refuse both, the score is the score.

**Proposal C** scores in the eighties. It's also shaped like ours, which you should hold against it while reading this page — we designed our proposal around this scoring sheet because we wrote the scoring sheet. Grade us on whether the criteria are the right ones, not on which composite wins.

callout.title: Use the score to negotiate, not to decide
callout.body: A 58 with a fixable gap often beats an 80 you can't afford. Take the sheet back to the agency you liked and ask them to close the two lowest-scoring lines. The ones who can do that in a day are the ones worth hiring.

sections.h2: The omission that should disqualify a proposal outright
body: No baseline. Not "a weak baseline" — the complete absence of a stated number, frozen on a stated date, that both parties agree the work will be judged against.

Without it, month nine is a debate. The agency shows a traffic chart going up and to the right. You say leads feel the same. Neither of you can win, because nobody wrote down where you started. Every other flaw in a proposal is negotiable; this one makes the whole engagement unfalsifiable by design.

The fix is one paragraph. Name the metric — qualified leads from organic search is the usual right answer, organic revenue if you're transactional. Name where it's measured, which should be your CRM, not analytics. Freeze the trailing 90 days before kickoff. Name the date you'll both look at it again.

That paragraph is why we structure our own [SEO engagements](/seo) around a frozen trailing-90-day organic lead count rather than a ranking promise. We don't guarantee a position — nobody controls Google's index — but we do guarantee movement against your own number, and if we miss it in 90 days we keep working free until we beat it. Any agency can write that clause. Most choose not to, and that choice is information.

sections.h2: What to get in writing before you sign
body: Seven lines. If an agency can't supply all seven within two working days, you've learned something more useful than any proposal could tell you.
numbered: The baseline metric, its current value, the date it was frozen and where it's measured.
Named people, their roles, and the approximate hours each contributes per month.
Hours split across technical, content, links and reporting — see [what an SEO retainer includes](/answers/what-does-an-seo-retainer-include) for the shape this should take.
The last twenty links they placed for any client, as live URLs.
Who ships technical fixes, and what happens when something urgent breaks.
Notice period, minimum term, and confirmation that you own every asset and account on exit — the rest belongs in [your SEO contract](/answers/what-should-be-in-an-seo-contract).
What happens if the number doesn't move. Their answer to this is the single most predictive line in the document.

faqs.q: How do I compare SEO quotes with completely different deliverables?
faqs.a: Convert everything to hours, then divide the fee by the hours to get a blended rate. Four articles, ten technical fixes and twenty links all become numbers of working hours. Once every quote is expressed as hours per rupee, the comparison is arithmetic instead of vibes.

faqs.q: Is the cheapest SEO proposal always the worst?
faqs.a: No. A ₹25,000 quote for a small local site with a narrow keyword set can be perfectly honest. It becomes a problem when the deliverables list is impossible at that price — 30 links a month, unlimited keywords, eight articles. Check whether the arithmetic works before judging the number.

faqs.q: What does "unlimited keywords" actually mean in an SEO proposal?
faqs.a: It means the agency will track as many keywords as you like, which costs them almost nothing. The optimisation work is the same whether you track 20 or 2,000. Score it zero and ask instead how many queries the plan actively works on this quarter.

faqs.q: Should I pick the agency with the most detailed proposal?
faqs.a: Detail is a good proxy for whether they've planned the work, but length isn't. A three-page proposal with named people, itemised hours, real link samples and a frozen baseline beats a forty-page deck of methodology diagrams every time. Grade specificity, not page count.

faqs.q: How much should I weight price when comparing SEO proposals?
faqs.a: Around 12% in this sheet, expressed as hours per rupee rather than the headline fee. Price is the variable you can renegotiate later. Measurement, seniority and link sourcing are the ones you're stuck with, so they carry the weight.

faqs.q: Can I show one agency's proposal to another?
faqs.a: Show the scope sheet, not the document. Sharing a competitor's pricing is bad form and usually breaches their confidentiality line. Sharing your normalised requirements — hours, disciplines, baseline, contract terms — is fair, and it gets you three quotes you can actually compare.
